title: Partnership
shortDescription: Profit splits by capital × time, not by capital alone — the moment one partner's money sits in the business for a different length of time, plain investment ratios stop working.
genZNote: Money talks, but time gets a vote too. A partner's share is capital × time, not just capital — equal investment for less time isn't an equal share.

sections.heading: Core Idea
sections.body: Profit share in a partnership is proportional to (Investment × Time period invested) for each partner — NOT to investment alone, unless every partner invested for exactly the same duration, in which case time cancels out of the ratio and investment alone is enough.

steps.name: Set up capital-time products
steps.explanation: A invests ₹4000 for 12 months; B invests ₹6000 for 8 months. Total profit ₹3400. A's capital-time = 4000×12 = 48000. B's capital-time = 6000×8 = 48000.
steps.purpose: Convert each partner's contribution into a single comparable number.

steps.name: Divide by the ratio
steps.purpose: Despite B investing 50% more capital, the shorter duration exactly balances it out to an equal split.

sections.heading: Partner Joining, Leaving, or Changing Investment
sections.body: If a partner's investment changes partway through the year (extra capital added, partial withdrawal, or a new partner joins later), split that partner's contribution into separate capital-time segments and add them — do not average the investment amount over the full period.

sections.heading: When Efficiency Differs
sections.body: Some partnership problems (especially where 'sleeping' vs 'working' partners are involved) specify a partner does 'extra' work beyond capital contribution — treat that as a separate agreed share (often a fixed management fee taken off the top before splitting the remaining profit by capital-time) rather than folding it into the capital-time ratio.

sections.heading: Common Traps
bullets: Dividing profit purely by investment amount, ignoring duration — only valid when every partner invested for the same length of time.
Averaging a changed investment amount over the full period instead of splitting it into separate capital-time segments.
Forgetting to convert all time periods to the same unit (months vs years) before multiplying.

sections.heading: Exam Strategy
bullets: Always compute capital × time for each partner as the first step, even if the times look equal at first glance — read carefully for a mid-year change.
Simplify the capital-time ratio to its lowest terms before splitting the profit — smaller numbers reduce arithmetic mistakes.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Partnership profit splits in the ratio of (Investment × Time invested) for each partner, not investment alone, unless all durations are equal.
keyFacts: If all partners invest for the same duration, the time term cancels and capital ratio alone is correct.
A changed investment mid-period splits into separate capital-time segments added together.
commonConfusion: Equal capital does not mean equal share if the investment durations differ — and vice versa, unequal capital can still produce an equal share if durations offset the difference.

highYieldFacts: Profit ratio = capital × time for each partner, always — check whether durations are actually equal before simplifying to capital alone.
commonTraps: Using investment ratio alone when durations actually differ.
Averaging instead of segmenting a mid-period investment change.
mustRemember: Convert every time period to the same unit before multiplying by capital.
